name: First Indochina War
summary: The communist-led Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh and General Vo Nguyen Giap fought France, which sought to restore its colonial rule over Indochina after the Second World War. A guerrilla war in the hills of Tonkin grew, with Chinese aid after 1949, into a conventional war that ended with the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The Geneva Accords divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, setting the stage for the Vietnam War.

steps.label: Mar to Dec 1946
steps.title: War breaks out in Tonkin
steps.text: General Leclerc's troops sailed from Saigon and landed at Haiphong in March 1946 as talks with Ho Chi Minh's government faltered. In November a customs dispute led the French navy to shell Haiphong, and on 19 December the Viet Minh attacked the French in Hanoi. After weeks of street fighting Giap withdrew his forces to the mountain base of the Viet Bac.

events.name: Bombardment of Haiphong
events.text: French warships shelled the port in November 1946, killing thousands of Vietnamese civilians.

events.name: Battle of Hanoi
events.text: The Viet Minh rising of 19 December began the war; French troops held the city after two months of fighting.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 1947
steps.title: Operation Lea
steps.text: General Salan tried to end the war at a stroke by dropping paratroopers on the Viet Minh headquarters at Bac Kan while armoured and river columns closed in from Lang Son and the Clear River. Ho Chi Minh and Giap escaped, and the Viet Minh melted into the jungle. France held the cities and the deltas while the Viet Minh ruled the countryside of the north.

moves.label: River column up the Clear River

events.name: Operation Lea
events.text: French paratroopers seized Bac Kan but narrowly missed capturing Ho Chi Minh.

steps.label: Sep to Oct 1950
steps.title: Disaster on Route 4
steps.text: Communist victory in China in 1949 gave the Viet Minh a safe rear and a supply of weapons and advisers. In 1950 Giap's new regular divisions attacked the French border posts along Route 4, destroying the columns evacuating Cao Bang. France abandoned Lang Son and the whole northern frontier.

events.name: Battle of Route Coloniale 4
events.text: The Viet Minh destroyed two French columns near Dong Khe, France's worst colonial defeat to that date.

steps.label: 1951 to 1952
steps.title: De Lattre holds the delta
steps.text: General de Lattre took command and ringed the Red River Delta with a chain of concrete forts, the De Lattre Line. Giap's attempts to break into the delta at Vinh Yen, Mao Khe and the Day River were thrown back by French firepower. A French thrust to Hoa Binh in late 1951 was itself forced back, and the war settled into a bloody deadlock.

events.name: Battle of Vinh Yen
events.text: French air power and napalm broke Giap's first set-piece offensive in January 1951.

events.name: Battle of Hoa Binh
events.text: The French withdrew from Hoa Binh in February 1952 after heavy losses.

steps.label: 1952 to 1953
steps.title: War spreads to Laos
steps.text: Giap shifted the war into the thinly held highlands of northwest Tonkin and in April 1953 invaded Laos, threatening Luang Prabang. The French had beaten off attacks at the fortified airhead of Na San, and General Navarre decided to repeat that model. In November 1953 paratroopers dropped into the valley of Dien Bien Phu to block the road to Laos.

events.name: Battle of Na San
events.text: The airlifted garrison repulsed Viet Minh assaults, inspiring the plan for Dien Bien Phu.

events.name: Operation Castor
events.text: French paratroopers seized Dien Bien Phu on 20 November 1953.

steps.label: Mar to Jul 1954
steps.title: Dien Bien Phu and Geneva
steps.text: Giap hauled artillery through the mountains and ringed Dien Bien Phu with some 50,000 troops. From 13 March his guns closed the airstrip and the strongpoints fell one by one until the garrison under Colonel de Castries surrendered on 7 May. At Geneva in July, France agreed to leave, and Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel pending elections.

events.name: Battle of Dien Bien Phu
events.text: The 57-day siege ended with the surrender of about 11,000 French Union troops.

events.name: Geneva Accords
events.text: Signed at Geneva on 21 July, they ended French rule and split Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

name: 1948 Arab-Israeli War
summary: After the United Nations voted in November 1947 to partition British Mandate Palestine, fighting broke out between Jewish and Palestinian Arab forces, and when Israel declared independence in May 1948 the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon intervened. Israel won the war and the 1949 armistice lines left it with more territory than the partition plan, while Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt the Gaza Strip. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an exodus Palestinians call the Nakba, and the refugee question remains unresolved.

sides.name: Arab states and Palestinian Arab forces

steps.label: Nov 1947 to Mar 1948
steps.title: Partition and civil war
steps.text: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted to partition Palestine into Jewish and Arab states, with Jerusalem under international rule. The Jewish leadership accepted and the Arab leadership rejected the plan, and fighting broke out at once between the Haganah and Palestinian Arab irregulars. Arab forces under Abd al-Qadir al-Husseini cut the road to Jerusalem, besieging its Jewish population, while Fawzi al-Qawuqji's Arab Liberation Army entered the north.

moves.label: Army of the Holy War blockades the Jerusalem road
Arab Liberation Army enters from Syria

events.name: Siege of Jerusalem
events.text: Ambushes at Bab al-Wad cut off the 100,000 Jews of Jerusalem from the coast.

steps.label: Apr to mid May 1948
steps.title: The Haganah offensive
steps.text: In April the Haganah went on the offensive under Plan Dalet, opening the Jerusalem road in Operation Nachshon and killing Abd al-Qadir at al-Qastal. On 9 April Irgun and Lehi fighters killed over 100 villagers at Deir Yassin, and Haifa and Jaffa fell soon after. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes, the start of the Nakba.

events.name: Battle of al-Qastal
events.text: Abd al-Qadir al-Husseini was killed and the Palestinian forces around Jerusalem lost their leader.

events.name: Deir Yassin massacre
events.text: Irgun and Lehi fighters killed over 100 Palestinian villagers, spreading fear across the country.

events.name: Fall of Haifa
events.text: Haganah forces took the port city and most of its 70,000 Arab residents left.

steps.label: 15 May to 11 Jun 1948
steps.title: The Arab armies invade
steps.text: Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 as the British Mandate ended. The next day the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered. The Egyptians drove up the coast to Isdud, Glubb's Arab Legion took the Old City of Jerusalem and held Latrun, and the Syrians were stopped at Degania, until a UN truce began on 11 June.

moves.label: Syrian attack in the Jordan Valley

events.name: Battles of Latrun
events.text: The Arab Legion repulsed repeated Israeli attacks on the fort guarding the Jerusalem road.

events.name: Fall of the Jewish Quarter
events.text: The Arab Legion took the Old City of Jerusalem on 28 May.

events.name: Battle of Degania
events.text: Kibbutz defenders stopped the Syrian advance south of the Sea of Galilee.

steps.label: Jul 1948
steps.title: The Ten Days
steps.text: Israel used the truce to import arms and returned to battle stronger. In ten days of fighting in July, Yigal Allon's Operation Danny took Lydda and Ramle, whose tens of thousands of Arab residents were expelled, and Operation Dekel took Nazareth. A second truce in July froze the lines, and in September the UN mediator Count Bernadotte was assassinated in Jerusalem by Lehi militants.

events.name: Lydda and Ramle
events.text: Israeli forces took both towns and expelled some 50,000 to 70,000 Palestinian residents.

events.name: Assassination of Count Bernadotte
events.text: The UN mediator was killed by Lehi gunmen on 17 September.

steps.label: Oct 1948 to Jan 1949
steps.title: Negev and Galilee offensives
steps.text: In October Allon's Operation Yoav broke through the Egyptian lines and took Beersheba, trapping an Egyptian brigade in the Faluja pocket. Operation Hiram drove the Arab Liberation Army out of the upper Galilee into Lebanon. In Operation Horev in December, Israeli forces pushed the Egyptians out of the Negev and briefly into Sinai before British pressure forced a withdrawal.

events.name: Capture of Beersheba
events.text: Israeli forces took the Negev's main town on 21 October.

events.name: Faluja pocket
events.text: A surrounded Egyptian brigade, including Gamal Abdel Nasser, held out until the armistice.

steps.label: Feb to Jul 1949
steps.title: Armistice lines
steps.text: Under UN mediator Ralph Bunche, Israel signed armistice agreements at Rhodes with Egypt in February, Lebanon in March, Jordan in April and Syria in July. In March an Israeli column reached the Red Sea at Umm al-Rashrash, later Eilat. The armistice lines, later called the Green Line, left Jordan in the West Bank and East Jerusalem and Egypt in the Gaza Strip, while about 700,000 Palestinian refugees were not allowed to return.

moves.label: Operation Uvda to the Red Sea

events.name: Armistice agreements at Rhodes
events.text: The 1949 agreements ended the fighting but were not peace treaties.

events.name: Nakba
events.text: Some 700,000 Palestinians became refugees, many of them in Gaza, the West Bank and neighbouring countries.

name: Korean War
summary: North Korea, backed by the Soviet Union and later joined by Chinese troops, invaded South Korea, which was defended by the United States and a United Nations coalition. After dramatic swings up and down the peninsula the war settled into a stalemate near the 38th parallel, and an armistice in 1953 left Korea divided. About three million people died, and the war hardened Cold War divisions in Asia that persist today.

steps.label: Jun to Sep 1950
steps.title: North Korea invades
steps.text: On 25 June 1950 the Korean People's Army crossed the 38th parallel with Soviet-built tanks and captured Seoul within days. The UN Security Council authorised military help, but the first US units were brushed aside at Osan and Daejeon. By August General Walker's Eighth Army and the South Korean army were penned into a perimeter around Busan behind the Naktong River.

events.name: First Battle of Seoul
events.text: North Korean forces captured the South Korean capital three days into the war.

events.name: Battle of the Pusan Perimeter
events.text: UN forces held the line of the Naktong River for six weeks.

steps.label: Sep 1950
steps.title: The Inchon landing
steps.text: MacArthur landed General Almond's X Corps far behind enemy lines at Inchon on 15 September, cutting North Korean supply lines. Walker's Eighth Army broke out of the Busan perimeter, and Seoul was recaptured by the end of the month. The North Korean army collapsed and fled back across the 38th parallel.

events.name: Battle of Inchon
events.text: A bold amphibious landing turned the course of the war.

events.name: Second Battle of Seoul
events.text: US Marines and South Korean troops retook the capital after street fighting.

steps.label: Oct to Nov 1950
steps.title: UN advance to the Yalu
steps.text: UN forces crossed the 38th parallel to unify Korea, took Pyongyang on 19 October and pushed toward the Chinese border on the Yalu, while X Corps landed on the east coast at Wonsan. China, warning against the advance, secretly sent large forces under Peng Dehuai into Korea and struck the first blows at Unsan.

moves.label: X Corps by sea to Wonsan

events.name: Capture of Pyongyang
events.text: UN forces took the North Korean capital on 19 October.

events.name: Battle of Unsan
events.text: Chinese troops mauled US and South Korean units in their first major attack.

steps.label: Nov 1950 to Jan 1951
steps.title: China intervenes
steps.text: Massive Chinese offensives in bitter cold routed the Eighth Army on the Chongchon River and surrounded US Marines at the Chosin Reservoir, who fought their way out to the coast and were evacuated from Hungnam. UN forces retreated south of the 38th parallel, and Seoul fell again in January 1951.

events.name: Battle of the Chongchon River
events.text: Chinese attacks broke the Eighth Army and forced the longest retreat in US Army history.

events.name: Battle of Chosin Reservoir
events.text: US Marines and soldiers broke out of encirclement in brutal cold, but China regained northeast Korea.

events.name: Third Battle of Seoul
events.text: Chinese and North Korean forces recaptured Seoul in January 1951.

steps.label: Feb to Jun 1951
steps.title: Ridgway strikes back
steps.text: Under General Ridgway, who took over after Walker's death, UN forces held at Chipyong-ni and pushed north again, retaking Seoul in March. Truman dismissed MacArthur in April for publicly demanding a wider war with China. China's spring offensive in April and May was stopped short of Seoul, and the front stabilised near the 38th parallel.

events.name: Battle of Chipyong-ni
events.text: Surrounded US and French troops held off Chinese attacks, restoring UN morale.

events.name: Battle of Kapyong
events.text: Commonwealth troops blunted the Chinese spring offensive in the centre.

steps.label: Jul 1951 to 1953
steps.title: Stalemate and the hill battles
steps.text: Armistice talks opened at Kaesong and moved to Panmunjom while both sides fought costly battles for hills along a fortified front much like the trenches of the First World War. US bombing devastated North Korea. The fate of prisoners who did not want to go home was the main sticking point in the talks.

events.name: Battle of Heartbreak Ridge
events.text: UN forces took the ridge after a month of fighting with heavy losses.

events.name: Battle of Triangle Hill
events.text: Chinese forces held their positions after six weeks of fighting.

steps.label: Jul 1953
steps.title: Armistice
steps.text: A final Chinese offensive at Kumsong pushed back South Korean lines weeks before the armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. It created the Demilitarized Zone along the final front line near the 38th parallel. No peace treaty has ever been signed.

events.name: Battle of Kumsong
events.text: The last major Chinese offensive gained ground before the ceasefire.

events.name: Korean Armistice Agreement
events.text: Signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953, it ended the fighting without a peace treaty.

name: Mau Mau uprising
summary: Mau Mau fighters, mostly Kikuyu, rose against British colonial rule in Kenya over land taken by white settlers and political exclusion. Britain declared an emergency, crushed the forest armies with troops, loyalist Home Guards and the mass detention of tens of thousands of Kikuyu, and by 1956 the revolt was broken. Over 11,000 rebels and about 200 members of the security forces died along with many civilians, and abuses in the camps helped persuade Britain to grant Kenya independence in 1963.

sides.name: Mau Mau (Kenya Land and Freedom Army)

steps.label: Oct 1952
steps.title: State of emergency
steps.text: After a wave of killings of loyalist Kikuyu, Governor Evelyn Baring declared a state of emergency on 20 October 1952. In Operation Jock Scott police arrested Jomo Kenyatta and about 180 other nationalist leaders, and British troops were flown in from the Canal Zone. Thousands of young Kikuyu went into the forests of the Aberdares and Mount Kenya to fight.

events.name: Operation Jock Scott
events.text: Kenyatta and other leaders were arrested on the first night of the emergency.

steps.title: Lari and the war in the forests
steps.text: On 26 March 1953 Mau Mau fighters attacked the loyalist village of Lari, killing over 70 people, and security forces and Home Guards killed many suspects in reprisals. General Erskine arrived in June to run the army campaign. At Kapenguria Kenyatta was convicted of managing Mau Mau, a charge he always denied, and jailed.

events.name: Lari massacre
events.text: Mau Mau killed over 70 loyalist villagers, and reprisals killed many more.

events.name: Kapenguria trial
events.text: Kenyatta and five others were sentenced to seven years' hard labour.

steps.label: Apr 1954
steps.title: Operation Anvil
steps.text: General China was captured in January 1954. In April Erskine sealed off Nairobi, the movement's source of recruits, money and supplies, and screened its whole African population. About 20,000 Kikuyu were sent to detention camps, and hundreds of thousands more in the countryside were forced into guarded villages.

moves.label: Detainees sent to Langata and Manyani camps

events.name: Operation Anvil
events.text: The sweep of Nairobi cut the forest fighters off from their urban supporters.

steps.label: 1955 to 1956
steps.title: The hunt for Kimathi
steps.text: With a ditch and patrols sealing the forest edge, Operations Hammer and First Flute swept the Aberdares and Mount Kenya. Small pseudo gangs of turned fighters led by police officers like Ian Henderson tracked down the remaining bands. Dedan Kimathi was shot and captured near Nyeri on 21 October 1956 and hanged in 1957, which ended the armed revolt.

moves.label: Operation First Flute on Mount Kenya

events.name: Capture of Dedan Kimathi
events.text: The last major Mau Mau leader was wounded and captured near Nyeri.

steps.label: Mar 1959
steps.title: Hola massacre
steps.text: Tens of thousands remained in detention camps where screening often involved beatings and torture. On 3 March 1959 guards at Hola camp beat eleven detainees to death. The cover-up and its exposure caused an uproar in the British Parliament and hastened the end of the emergency.

events.name: Hola massacre
events.text: Eleven detainees were beaten to death by guards, a scandal that shook the colonial government.

steps.label: Jan 1960
steps.title: End of the emergency
steps.text: The emergency was lifted in January 1960, and that same month the Lancaster House conference in London opened the way to African majority rule. Kenyatta was released in 1961 and led Kenya to independence in December 1963. Many survivors of the camps waited decades for recognition, until Britain paid compensation in 2013.

events.name: Emergency lifted
events.text: The end of the emergency in January 1960 opened the road to independence in 1963.

name: Algerian War
summary: The National Liberation Front (FLN) fought for independence from France, which regarded Algeria, home to about a million European settlers, as part of France itself. The French army largely defeated the guerrillas inside Algeria through mass troop deployments, border barriers and widespread torture, but the war broke the Fourth Republic and brought de Gaulle to power. De Gaulle negotiated Algerian independence in 1962 after a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Algerians and drove most settlers to France.

steps.label: Nov 1954 to 1955
steps.title: Toussaint Rouge
steps.text: On 1 November 1954 the newly formed FLN launched coordinated attacks across Algeria, strongest in the Aures mountains under Mostefa Ben Boulaid. France answered that Algeria was France and poured in troops. In August 1955 FLN-led crowds killed over 120 people, most of them European settlers, around Philippeville, and French reprisals killed thousands of Muslim Algerians, turning the revolt into a full war.

events.name: Toussaint Rouge
events.text: Some 30 attacks on 1 November 1954 began the war.

events.name: Philippeville massacre
events.text: FLN-led killings of settlers were followed by reprisals that killed thousands of Algerians.

steps.label: 1956 to 1957
steps.title: The Battle of Algiers
steps.text: At the Soummam Congress in August 1956 the FLN organised its army and political leadership, and from late 1956 it waged a bombing campaign in Algiers. In January 1957 General Massu's 10th Parachute Division took over the city, breaking the FLN network through mass arrests and systematic torture. Larbi Ben M'hidi was captured and killed in custody, and by October the battle was won, at a high political cost to France.

events.name: Soummam Congress
events.text: The FLN set up its leadership and structure in a secret meeting in Kabylie.

events.name: Battle of Algiers
events.text: French paratroopers dismantled the FLN in the capital, using widespread torture.

steps.label: 1957 to 1958
steps.title: Sealing the borders
steps.text: Independent Tunisia and Morocco became bases for the FLN's external army. France built the electrified Morice Line along the Tunisian border and a similar barrier facing Morocco, and in the battle of the frontiers in early 1958 destroyed most ALN units trying to cross. In May 1958 settlers and generals seized power in Algiers, and the crisis brought Charles de Gaulle back to power in Paris.

events.name: Battle of Souk Ahras
events.text: French troops destroyed an ALN battalion crossing the Morice Line in April 1958.

events.name: Bombing of Sakiet Sidi Youssef
events.text: French aircraft bombed a Tunisian border village, causing an international outcry.

events.name: May 1958 crisis
events.text: A settler and army revolt in Algiers ended the Fourth Republic and recalled de Gaulle.

steps.label: 1959 to 1960
steps.title: The Challe Plan
steps.text: General Challe's mobile reserves swept the country from west to east, from the Oran region through the Ouarsenis to Kabylie and the Constantine mountains, and broke up most ALN units inside Algeria. Yet de Gaulle concluded that military victory could not settle the question and in September 1959 offered Algerians self-determination. Settler ultras rose against him in Algiers in the Week of the Barricades in January 1960.

events.name: Operation Jumelles
events.text: French forces swept Kabylie, the FLN's heartland, from July 1959.

steps.title: Generals' putsch and the OAS
steps.text: After a referendum backed self-determination, four retired generals led by Challe and Salan seized Algiers on 22 April 1961 with the 1st Foreign Parachute Regiment. Conscripts and the public in France refused to follow them and the putsch collapsed in four days. Die-hards formed the OAS, which waged a terror campaign in Algeria and France against Muslims and supporters of independence.

events.name: Generals' putsch
events.text: The army revolt against de Gaulle failed after four days.

events.name: Paris massacre of 1961
events.text: Police killed scores of Algerian demonstrators in Paris on 17 October.

steps.label: Mar to Jul 1962
steps.title: Evian Accords and independence
steps.text: France and the FLN signed the Evian Accords on 18 March 1962, and a ceasefire followed. Algerians voted for independence, declared on 5 July 1962, while about 800,000 pieds noirs left for France and thousands of harkis who had served France were killed. Boumediene's border army marched on Algiers and installed Ahmed Ben Bella as leader.

events.name: Evian Accords
events.text: The agreements ended the war and led to Algerian independence.

events.name: Algerian independence
events.text: Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962 after 132 years of French rule.

name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956
summary: A student demonstration in Budapest on 23 October 1956 grew into a nationwide revolt against Hungary's Soviet-backed communist regime. Insurgents fought Soviet tanks to a standstill, the reform communist Imre Nagy formed a government and declared Hungary neutral, but on 4 November a massive Soviet invasion crushed the revolution. About 2,500 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers died, some 200,000 Hungarians fled abroad, and Nagy was executed in 1958.

steps.label: 23 Oct 1956
steps.title: Uprising in Budapest
steps.text: Students marched through Budapest in support of reform in Poland and demanded free elections and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Crowds toppled the giant Stalin statue, and the secret police opened fire outside the radio building, turning the protest into an armed revolt. That night General Lashchenko's Soviet Special Corps rolled into the capital from its bases.

events.name: Siege of the Radio building
events.text: Insurgents armed by sympathetic soldiers and workers took the radio station after a night of fighting.

steps.label: 24 to 30 Oct 1956
steps.title: Fighting the tanks
steps.text: Young insurgents with rifles and petrol bombs fought Soviet tanks from strongholds such as the Corvin Passage, and on 25 October security forces fired on a crowd in front of Parliament. Workers' councils took over towns across the country. Imre Nagy became prime minister, announced a ceasefire on 28 October, and the Soviets pulled their troops out of Budapest.

events.name: Kossuth Square massacre
events.text: Shooting into a crowd outside Parliament on 25 October killed scores of people.

events.name: Battle of the Corvin Passage
events.text: Insurgents held the strongpoint against repeated Soviet tank attacks.

steps.label: 31 Oct to 3 Nov 1956
steps.title: Neutrality and the Soviet decision
steps.text: On 31 October the Soviet leadership under Khrushchev decided to crush the revolution while the West was distracted by the Suez Crisis. As fresh Soviet divisions poured across the borders from Ukraine and Romania, Nagy declared Hungary's neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact on 1 November. On the night of 3 November Defence Minister Pal Maleter was arrested by the KGB during negotiations at Tokol.

events.name: Declaration of neutrality
events.text: Nagy announced that Hungary was leaving the Warsaw Pact and appealed to the UN.

events.name: Arrest of Pal Maleter
events.text: The Soviets seized the Hungarian delegation at the negotiating table.

steps.label: 4 to 11 Nov 1956
steps.title: Operation Whirlwind
steps.text: Before dawn on 4 November Konev's armies stormed Budapest with thousands of tanks, while Janos Kadar announced a new government from Szolnok. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, and resistance in Csepel and the steel town of Dunapentele ended by 11 November. Some 200,000 Hungarians fled, most across the border to Austria, and Nagy was later abducted, tried in secret and hanged.

events.name: Battle of Budapest
events.text: Soviet forces crushed armed resistance in the capital within a week.

events.name: Fall of Csepel
events.text: The industrial island was the last stronghold in Budapest to surrender.

events.name: Kadar government proclaimed
events.text: Kadar's Soviet-backed government ruled Hungary until 1988.

name: Cuban Revolution
summary: Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement, alongside other opposition groups, waged a guerrilla war against the military dictatorship of Fulgencio Batista. From a small band in the Sierra Maestra mountains the rebels defeated Batista's much larger army in 1958, and Batista fled on 1 January 1959. Castro's new government soon allied with the Soviet Union, making Cuba a Cold War flashpoint.

steps.label: 26 Jul 1953
steps.title: Attack on the Moncada Barracks
steps.text: Fidel Castro led about 160 young rebels in an attack on the Moncada army barracks in Santiago de Cuba, hoping to spark a rising against Batista, who had seized power in a 1952 coup. The attack failed, many captured rebels were killed, and Castro was tried and jailed. His defence speech, ending History will absolve me, made him famous, and the movement took its name from the date.

events.name: Moncada Barracks attack
events.text: The assault failed and dozens of rebels were killed, many after capture.

steps.label: Nov to Dec 1956
steps.title: The Granma landing
steps.text: Freed in an amnesty in 1955, Castro organised an expedition in Mexico. On 2 December 1956, 82 men landed from the overcrowded yacht Granma in a swamp near Niquero, days late for a planned rising led by Frank Pais in Santiago. Batista's army scattered them at Alegria de Pio, and about 20 survivors, including Fidel and Raul Castro and Che Guevara, regrouped in the Sierra Maestra.

events.name: Battle of Alegria de Pio
events.text: Government troops ambushed and scattered the expedition three days after the landing.

steps.title: Guerrillas in the Sierra
steps.text: The small guerrilla band won its first fight at La Plata in January 1957 and gained recruits among mountain peasants, while a New York Times interview made Castro known abroad. In Havana the student Directorio Revolucionario stormed the Presidential Palace in March but failed to kill Batista. In May the rebels overran the army post at El Uvero, and Batista's repression in the cities turned more Cubans against him.

events.name: Attack on the Presidential Palace
events.text: José Antonio Echeverría and dozens of student rebels were killed.

events.name: Battle of El Uvero
events.text: The rebels' first major victory took an army garrison on the coast.

steps.label: Mar to Aug 1958
steps.title: Batista's summer offensive
steps.text: Raul Castro opened a second front in the Sierra Cristal in March 1958. In May Batista launched Operation Verano, sending some 10,000 troops under General Cantillo against about 300 guerrillas in the Sierra Maestra. The rebels used ambushes and the mountains to defeat the columns one by one, including at El Jigue, and by August the army had withdrawn, demoralised.

moves.label: Second front in the Sierra Cristal

events.name: Battle of La Plata and El Jigue
events.text: A surrounded army battalion surrendered to Castro's guerrillas in July.

events.name: Operation Verano fails
events.text: Batista's army abandoned the offensive and lost the initiative for good.

steps.label: Aug 1958 to Jan 1959
steps.title: The march west and Santa Clara
steps.text: In August Che Guevara and Camilo Cienfuegos led columns west across Camaguey to the Escambray mountains in central Cuba. In late December Guevara's column took Santa Clara, derailing an armoured train, which cut the island in two. Batista fled to the Dominican Republic on 1 January 1959, and Castro entered Havana on 8 January after a victory march across the island.

events.name: Battle of Santa Clara
events.text: Guevara's victory and the capture of the armoured train sealed Batista's fate.

events.name: Batista flees
events.text: Batista left Cuba in the early hours of 1 January 1959.

name: Vietnam War
summary: Communist North Vietnam and the southern Viet Cong insurgency fought South Vietnam and its chief ally the United States to reunify the country under communist rule. US combat troops arrived in 1965 and withdrew in 1973 after a costly, divisive war, and North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon in April 1975. Millions of Vietnamese and over 58,000 Americans died, and the war spread to Laos and Cambodia and reshaped US foreign policy and society.

steps.label: 1955 to 1958
steps.title: Two Vietnams
steps.text: The 1954 Geneva Accords split Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with Ho Chi Minh's communist government in the North. In the South, Ngo Dinh Diem founded the Republic of Vietnam in 1955 with American backing and refused to hold the reunification elections planned for 1956. Nearly a million people, many of them Catholics, moved from North to South.

events.name: Republic of Vietnam proclaimed
events.text: Diem won a rigged referendum and proclaimed the republic in Saigon in October 1955.

steps.label: 1959 to 1963
steps.title: The insurgency grows
steps.text: In 1959 Hanoi approved armed struggle in the South and began building the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos. The National Liberation Front, known as the Viet Cong, was founded in 1960, and US military advisers grew to about 16,000 by 1963. After Buddhist protests, Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963, leaving the South in turmoil.

events.name: Battle of Ap Bac
events.text: A Viet Cong battalion beat off a much larger South Vietnamese force with US advisers.

events.name: Overthrow of Diem
events.text: Generals seized power in Saigon on 1 November 1963 and killed Diem.

steps.label: Aug 1964 to 1965
steps.title: American escalation
steps.text: After a clash between US destroyers and North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin, Congress gave President Johnson broad war powers. In 1965 the US began sustained bombing of the North and landed Marines at Da Nang, and under General Westmoreland US troop numbers rose to over 180,000 by the end of the year. In the Ia Drang valley US and North Vietnamese regulars met in their first big battle.

moves.label: US Marines land at Da Nang
1st Cavalry Division air assault into Ia Drang

events.name: Gulf of Tonkin incident
events.text: North Vietnamese boats attacked USS Maddox; a second reported attack two days later probably never happened.

events.name: Battle of Ia Drang
events.text: The first major battle between US and North Vietnamese regular troops; both sides claimed success.

steps.label: Jan to Apr 1968
steps.title: The Tet Offensive
steps.text: While Giap's divisions besieged the Marine base at Khe Sanh, the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese attacked over 100 towns and cities during the Tet holiday, including the US embassy in Saigon. The offensive was beaten back with very heavy communist losses, and at Hue communist forces executed thousands of civilians. But it shocked the American public and led President Johnson to limit bombing and seek talks.

events.name: Siege of Khe Sanh
events.text: The Marine base held through a 77-day siege and was abandoned a few months later.

events.name: Battle of Hue
events.text: US and South Vietnamese troops retook the old imperial city after nearly a month of street fighting.

events.name: Tet attacks on Saigon
events.text: Attackers in Saigon were defeated within days, but the shock was enormous.

steps.label: 1969 to 1971
steps.title: Vietnamization and a wider war
steps.text: President Nixon began withdrawing US troops while handing the fighting to the South Vietnamese army, under General Abrams. US and South Vietnamese forces struck communist bases in Cambodia in 1970, sparking mass protests in the United States, and a South Vietnamese incursion into Laos in 1971 to cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail was driven back.

events.name: Cambodian campaign
events.text: US and South Vietnamese troops seized supply caches but did not destroy the communist command.

events.name: Operation Lam Son 719
events.text: South Vietnamese forces reached Tchepone in Laos but retreated under heavy attack.

steps.label: Mar 1972 to Mar 1973
steps.title: Easter Offensive and the Paris Accords
steps.text: North Vietnam launched a conventional invasion across the DMZ and from Laos and Cambodia with tanks and artillery. South Vietnamese forces, backed by massive US air power, held An Loc and Kontum and retook Quang Tri. After the Christmas bombing of Hanoi, the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 brought the last US troops home, but North Vietnamese forces stayed in the South.

events.name: Battle of An Loc
events.text: The besieged town held for two months, blocking the road to Saigon.

events.name: Second Battle of Quang Tri
events.text: The city fell in May and South Vietnamese troops retook its ruins in September.

events.name: Paris Peace Accords
events.text: Signed in Paris in January 1973, they ended direct US involvement but not the war.

steps.label: Mar to Apr 1975
steps.title: Fall of Saigon
steps.text: General Van Tien Dung's final offensive began in the Central Highlands at Ban Me Thuot, and a disorderly South Vietnamese retreat lost Hue and Da Nang. After a last stand at Xuan Loc, North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon on 30 April 1975 as the last Americans were evacuated by helicopter. Vietnam was formally reunified in 1976.

moves.label: Ho Chi Minh Campaign on Saigon

events.name: Battle of Ban Me Thuot
events.text: The surprise capture of the city triggered the collapse of the South Vietnamese army.

events.name: Battle of Xuan Loc
events.text: South Vietnam's 18th Division held for nearly two weeks before withdrawing.

events.name: Fall of Saigon
events.text: North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon and South Vietnam surrendered.

name: Six-Day War
summary: After weeks of rising tension, in which Egypt expelled UN peacekeepers from Sinai and closed the Straits of Tiran, Israel launched a pre-emptive strike on 5 June 1967. In six days it defeated Egypt, Jordan and Syria and took the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. The war tripled the territory Israel controlled, displaced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians and Syrians, and shaped Middle East politics for decades.

steps.label: May to 4 Jun 1967
steps.title: Crisis
steps.text: Amid Syrian border clashes and Soviet reports of Israeli troop concentrations, Nasser moved divisions into Sinai, had the UN peacekeepers withdrawn and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Jordan signed a defence pact with Egypt and Iraqi troops moved toward Jordan. Israel mobilised its reserves and made Moshe Dayan defence minister on 1 June.

events.name: Closure of the Straits of Tiran
events.text: Israel had long declared a blockade of its Red Sea port of Eilat a cause for war.

steps.label: 5 to 8 Jun 1967
steps.title: Air strike and the Sinai
steps.text: On the morning of 5 June the Israeli air force destroyed most of Egypt's air force on the ground in Operation Focus. Israel Tal's division broke through at Rafah to El Arish, Ariel Sharon's took the fortified Abu Ageila position, and Avraham Yoffe's tanks crossed the dunes between them. Amer ordered a general retreat on 6 June, which turned into a rout, and Israeli forces reached the Suez Canal and Sharm el-Sheikh by 8 June.

moves.label: Through the dunes to Bir Lahfan

events.name: Operation Focus
events.text: Israeli air strikes destroyed about 300 Egyptian aircraft in three hours.

events.name: Battle of Abu Ageila
events.text: Sharon's night assault broke Egypt's main fortified position in Sinai.

steps.label: 5 to 7 Jun 1967
steps.title: Jerusalem and the West Bank
steps.text: Jordan, under Egyptian General Abdul Munim Riad, opened fire along the Jerusalem front on 5 June. Israeli forces under Uzi Narkiss counterattacked, Mordechai Gur's paratroopers fought through Ammunition Hill and took the Old City on 7 June, and Elad Peled's division took Jenin and Nablus. The Jordanian army withdrew across the Jordan River, and some 200,000 to 300,000 Palestinians fled to Jordan.

moves.label: Harel Brigade to Ramallah and Jericho

events.name: Battle of Ammunition Hill
events.text: Paratroopers took the fortified Jordanian position in hand-to-hand fighting.

events.name: Capture of the Old City
events.text: Israeli paratroopers reached the Western Wall on 7 June.

steps.label: 9 to 10 Jun 1967
steps.title: Golan Heights and ceasefire
steps.text: With Egypt and Jordan out of the war, David Elazar's Northern Command stormed the Golan Heights on 9 June, where the Golani Brigade took the fortress of Tel Faher. Syrian defences collapsed, Quneitra fell on 10 June, and a UN ceasefire took effect that evening. In November UN Resolution 242 called for Israeli withdrawal from occupied territories in exchange for peace.

events.name: Battle of Tel Faher
events.text: The Golani Brigade took the fortified position after heavy fighting.

events.name: Fall of Quneitra
events.text: The capture of the Golan's main town ended the war on the Syrian front.

events.name: UN ceasefire
events.text: Fighting ended on 10 June with Israel holding Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan.

name: Nigerian Civil War
summary: After coups and massacres of Igbo people in the north, Nigeria's Eastern Region declared independence as the Republic of Biafra under Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu in May 1967. Federal forces under General Yakubu Gowon slowly encircled and blockaded the Biafran heartland, and Biafra surrendered in January 1970. Between one and three million people died, most from famine under the blockade, which drew worldwide attention and gave rise to modern humanitarian relief work.

steps.label: May to Jul 1967
steps.title: Secession and police action
steps.text: Ojukwu proclaimed the Republic of Biafra at Enugu on 30 May 1967, after the killings of thousands of Igbo in the north in 1966. On 6 July federal troops crossed into the north of Biafra, taking Nsukka and Ogoja, while Benjamin Adekunle's marines seized the oil terminal at Bonny from the sea. Gowon expected a short police action.

events.name: Biafra declares independence
events.text: Ojukwu proclaimed the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967.

events.name: Fall of Nsukka
events.text: The university town was the first major Biafran town to fall.

steps.label: Aug to Oct 1967
steps.title: Midwest invasion and the fall of Enugu
steps.text: On 9 August a Biafran column under Victor Banjo swept across the Niger, took Benin City and drove west to Ore, alarming Lagos. Murtala Mohammed's new 2nd Division threw it back and retook Benin City in September. Federal troops captured the Biafran capital Enugu on 4 October and Adekunle took Calabar, though Murtala's attempts to cross the Niger at Onitsha failed.

events.name: Battle of Ore
events.text: Federal troops stopped the Biafran thrust toward Lagos.

events.name: Fall of Enugu
events.text: The loss of its capital forced Biafra to move its government to Umuahia.

steps.title: Encirclement and blockade
steps.text: Federal forces tightened the ring in 1968: Murtala's division took Onitsha by land in March, and Adekunle's 3rd Marine Commando Division took Port Harcourt in May, cutting Biafra off from the sea. Biafra won a notable ambush of a federal convoy at Abagana. Under the blockade famine killed huge numbers of people, and church and charity relief flights landed at night on a road strip at Uli.

events.name: Abagana ambush
events.text: Biafran troops destroyed a large federal supply convoy on 31 March 1968.

events.name: Fall of Port Harcourt
events.text: The loss of the port and airfield sealed Biafra's encirclement.

steps.title: The last stronghold
steps.text: Federal troops took Aba and Owerri in late 1968 and the new capital Umuahia in April 1969, but Biafran forces recaptured Owerri the same month. Biafra fought on in a shrinking enclave, supplied by the Uli airstrip and backed by a few countries such as France, Gabon and Tanzania, while Britain and the Soviet Union armed the federal side.

events.name: Fall of Umuahia
events.text: Biafra lost its second capital in April 1969.

events.name: Recapture of Owerri
events.text: Biafra's last major victory retook the town after a long siege.

steps.label: Dec 1969 to Jan 1970
steps.title: Collapse and surrender
steps.text: In Operation Tail-Wind, Olusegun Obasanjo's 3rd Marine Commando Division split the enclave, retook Owerri and overran the Uli airstrip. Ojukwu flew to exile in Ivory Coast on 11 January 1970, and Philip Effiong surrendered in Lagos on 15 January. Gowon declared no victor, no vanquished and promised reconciliation.

events.name: Fall of Uli
events.text: The loss of Biafra's last airstrip ended all outside supply.

events.name: Biafran surrender
events.text: Effiong formally surrendered in Lagos on 15 January 1970.
